title: Roots in a simple-root subspace are subsystem Weyl translates
statement:
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional $\mathbf Q$-vector space [def-weil-vector-space-dimension], and let $R\subseteq V\setminus\{0\}$ be finite and span $V$. For each $\alpha\in R$ let $c_\alpha:V\to\mathbf Q$ be linear, with $c_\alpha(\alpha)=2$, $c_\alpha(R)\subseteq\mathbf Z$, and with $s_\alpha(v)=v-c_\alpha(v)\alpha$ permuting $R$. Assume $R\cap\mathbf Q\alpha=\{\alpha,-\alpha\}$ for every $\alpha\in R$. Let $\Delta\subseteq R$ be a basis of $V$ such that every root has integer $\Delta$-coordinates all nonnegative or all nonpositive. For $I\subseteq\Delta$ let $W_I$ be the subgroup of $\operatorname{GL}_{\mathbf Q}(V)$ generated by the reflections $s_\alpha$ with $\alpha\in I$. Write $\mathbf Q I$ for the rational linear span and $\mathbf Z I$ for the additive subgroup generated by $I$. Then
$$R\cap\mathbf Q I=R\cap\mathbf Z I=\{w\alpha:w\in W_I,\ \alpha\in I\}.$$
Thus each root supported on $I$ is the image of a simple root in $I$ under a finite product of reflections with simple roots in $I$. The empty root system and $I=\varnothing$ are allowed.

source.place: Appendix C.12--C.22, printed pp.610--612, especially C.22, W times the base equals the roots, applied to the root system in the span of I. Proposition 21.90(b), p.453, identifies I as the corresponding subsystem base in the group formulation.

proof.text: For each root $a$, linearity and $c_a(a)=2$ give $c_a(s_ax)=-c_a(x)$, hence $s_a^2x=x$ and $s_a(a)=-a$. In particular $-R=R$. Let $W$ be the subgroup generated by all $s_a$, $a\in R$. Each element permutes $R$, and an element fixing every root fixes their rational span $V$. Thus the homomorphism $W\to\operatorname{Sym}(R)$ is injective; $W$ is finite. If $I=\varnothing$, both intersections in the conclusion are empty because $\mathbf QI=\mathbf ZI=\{0\}$ and $0\notin R$, as is the orbit set. This includes $R=\varnothing$, when spanning forces $V=0$. We may now assume $I\ne\varnothing$.

source.place: Appendix C.1, C.12, C.15, printed pp.607,610--611; explicit finite-permutation argument and empty cases.

proof.text: Using the given finite basis $\Delta$, write $x=\sum x_a a$ and put $B_0(x,y)=\sum_{a\in\Delta}x_a y_a$. This is rational, symmetric, bilinear and positive definite, since $B_0(x,x)$ is a sum of rational squares and is zero only when every coordinate is zero. Define $B(x,y)=\sum_{w\in W}B_0(wx,wy)$. The identity summand is strictly positive for $x\ne0$ and every other diagonal summand is nonnegative, so $B$ is positive definite. For $g\in W$, right multiplication permutes $W$, giving $B(gx,gy)=\sum_{w\in W}B_0(wgx,wgy)=B(x,y)$.

source.place: Appendix C.19, printed p.611: finite averaging formula, written over Q in the prescribed base.

proof.text: Invariance for $s_a$ and $s_a(a)=-a$ imply $-B(x,a)=B(s_ax,a)=B(x,a)-c_a(x)B(a,a)$. Consequently $c_a(x)=2B(x,a)/B(a,a)$ for every root $a$ and $x\in V$; division is valid because $B(a,a)>0$. Thus a positive value of $B(x,a)$ gives $c_a(x)>0$. This derives the relation for the prescribed functionals, without assuming any inner product in the hypotheses.

source.place: Appendix C.20 and formula (174), printed pp.609,611: the orthogonal-reflection formula derived from invariance.

proof.text: Write every root $b$ uniquely as $\sum_{a\in\Delta}n_a(b)a$, with integers $n_a(b)$ all of one sign. Since $\Delta$ is a basis and $I\subseteq\Delta$, membership in $\mathbf QI$ is equivalent to $n_a(b)=0$ for $a\notin I$. In that case the coordinates on $I$ are already integers, so $b\in\mathbf ZI$. Conversely $\mathbf ZI\subseteq\mathbf QI$ by definition, proving $R\cap\mathbf QI=R\cap\mathbf ZI$. Call a root positive when its coordinates are nonnegative, and set $h(b)=\sum n_a(b)$ for positive roots. Then $h(b)$ is a positive integer, because a root is nonzero. Every root is positive or the negative of a positive root, using $-R=R$.

source.place: Appendix C.21, printed p.612: integral same-sign coordinates in a base; coordinate restriction to I.

proof.text: For a positive root $b\in\mathbf QI$ which is not a member of $I$, expand $0<B(b,b)=\sum_{a\in I}n_a(b)B(b,a)$. Some $a\in I$ therefore has $n_a(b)>0$ and $B(b,a)>0$. Put $m=c_a(b)$. This is a strictly positive integer by the preceding formula and the assumed integrality on roots. The root $b'=s_ab=b-ma$ remains in $\mathbf QI$. There is some $d\in I\setminus\{a\}$ with $n_d(b)>0$: otherwise $b$ is a positive rational multiple of $a$, so reducedness would force $b=a$, contrary to $b\notin I$.

source.place: Appendix C.18--C.22, printed pp.611--612: agent-supplied height descent for the subsystem form of W times the base equals R, first calculation.

proof.text: The $d$-coordinate of $b'$ is $n_d(b)>0$, because subtracting $ma$ changes only the $a$-coordinate. The same-sign hypothesis for the root $b'$ now forces all its coordinates to be nonnegative. Thus $b'$ is positive, and $1\le h(b')=h(b)-m<h(b)$. This is the full descent calculation; it uses the base property for the actual root $s_ab$, not an unproved assertion that all positive roots remain positive under reflection.

source.place: Appendix C.21--C.22, printed p.612: agent-supplied height descent, sign and strict-decrease calculation.

proof.text: Strong induction on the positive integer $h(b)$ proves that every positive root in $\mathbf QI$ is $w\alpha$ with $w\in W_I$, $\alpha\in I$. If $b\in I$, take $w=1$ and $\alpha=b$. Otherwise the preceding descent gives $a\in I$ and a positive $b'=s_ab$ in $\mathbf QI$ of smaller height. Write $b'=w\alpha$ by induction; then $b=s_ab'=s_aw\alpha$ and $s_aw\in W_I$. The initial height $1$ has a unique coordinate $1$ and every other coordinate $0$, hence is a member of $I$. If $b$ is negative, apply the positive case to $-b=w\alpha$; then $b=-w\alpha=w(-\alpha)=w s_\alpha\alpha$, and $w s_\alpha\in W_I$. This proves the inclusion of either intersection in the orbit set, including the negative roots.

source.place: Appendix C.22, printed p.612: agent-supplied strong induction establishing the subsystem form of W times the base equals R.

proof.text: Conversely each generator $s_a$ for $a\in I$ preserves $R$ by assumption and maps $\mathbf QI$ into itself by $s_a(x)=x-c_a(x)a$. Its inverse is itself, so every element of the generated subgroup $W_I$ preserves both $R$ and $\mathbf QI$. Thus $w\alpha\in R\cap\mathbf QI$ whenever $w\in W_I$ and $\alpha\in I$. Combining this with the other inclusion and the equality of intersections proves the displayed three-way equality. A word in the generators and their inverses is a finite product of the same reflections since each is involutive, giving the last sentence of the statement.

source.place: Appendix C.12, C.15, C.22, printed pp.610--612: closure under the specified reflections and assembly.

proof_origin.place: Appendix C.19--C.22, printed pp.611--612; explicit rational averaging and height-descent proof of the subsystem specialization of C.22, rather than invoking its orbit assertion as a black box.

lean.statement: theorem root_subsystem_simple_orbits (V : Type u) [AddCommGroup V] [Module ℚ V] [FiniteDimensional ℚ V] (R : Set V) (hRfinite : R.Finite) (hRzero : (0 : V) ∉ R) (hRspan : Submodule.span ℚ R = ⊤) (c : R → V →ₗ[ℚ] ℚ) (hc2 : ∀ a : R, c a a.1 = 2) (hcint : ∀ a r : R, ∃ z : ℤ, c a r.1 = (z : ℚ)) (hcperm : ∀ a : R, Set.BijOn (Module.reflection (hc2 a)) R R) (hRline : ∀ a : R, R ∩ (Submodule.span ℚ {a.1} : Set V) = {a.1, -a.1}) (Δ : Set V) (hΔ : Δ ⊆ R) (b : Module.Basis Δ ℚ V) (hb : ∀ a : Δ, b a = a.1) (hcoords : ∀ r : R, ∃ n : Δ → ℤ, (∀ a : Δ, b.repr r.1 a = (n a : ℚ)) ∧ ((∀ a : Δ, 0 ≤ n a) ∨ (∀ a : Δ, n a ≤ 0))) (I : Set V) (hI : I ⊆ Δ) : R ∩ (Submodule.span ℚ I : Set V) = R ∩ (AddSubgroup.closure I : Set V) ∧ R ∩ (AddSubgroup.closure I : Set V) = {x : V | ∃ w : V ≃ₗ[ℚ] V, w ∈ Subgroup.closure {s : V ≃ₗ[ℚ] V | ∃ a : R, a.1 ∈ I ∧ s = Module.reflection (hc2 a)} ∧ ∃ a ∈ I, w a = x}
